Stock no dining tables and 133 chairs. This gives a profit of $9,975, the best the model finds with whole-number quantities. The floor space and the chair-share rule (at least 70% chairs) don't hold the result back, since leaving either one out or loosening it would not raise profit. The capital limit does constrain the result, even though $50 of it is unused: removing that limit would improve profit, but raising it by one unit would not, because whole-number quantities can't use a small amount of extra capital.

Make 20 chocolate cakes and 30 vanilla cakes each day, for a profit of $530. The bakery is limited by the 30-cake vanilla demand and the 50-cake daily production cap, and both are fully used. Making more vanilla cakes would be more profitable than chocolate cakes, but vanilla demand caps that at 30 and the production limit caps the total at 50. Chocolate demand (50) does not limit the result, since 30 of its allowance goes unused and loosening it would not help. The plan assumes the 30 vanilla cakes will sell and that the staff can produce 50 cakes a day.

Run 48 magazine ads, 8 flyers, and no billboard ads, which reaches an estimated 520,000 viewers. The city's cap of 8 flyers is the main limit: it is fully used, and allowing more flyers would improve the result. The $50,000 budget also constrains the plan, since removing it would improve the outcome, but the $400 left over and the whole-ad purchases mean one more dollar of budget would not help. The billboard-share and magazine-share rules do not limit the result, because removing either would not improve it.

Make about 10.11 units of peppers and 8.72 units of tomatoes, which gives the cheapest paste at a cost of about $124.47. This mix exactly meets the minimum of 130 spice units and 90 flavor units, with nothing left over. Each extra unit of required spice would raise the cost by about $0.57, and each extra unit of required flavor by about $0.55. The plan is limited by those two minimums, so any stricter requirement makes the paste more expensive.

Make 40 two-piece suits and 28 three-piece suits. This gives a profit of $46,400, the highest the model allows under whole-number production. Stitching time is fully used at 300 hours, and the store must make at least 40 two-piece suits, which this plan meets exactly. Measuring time has 54 hours left over, and removing that rule would not improve the result, so it is not what limits profit. Both stitching time and the 40-suit minimum do limit profit: removing either one would let the model do better, and making one more unit of either would not help.

Produce only the Premium grade, about 11.67 tons per month, and make no Standard or Plus alloy. This plan brings in a profit of about $64,167 per month. Zinc ore is the bottleneck: all 35 tons are used, while about 80 tons of iron ore sit unused, so extra iron would add nothing. Each additional ton of zinc ore would raise profit by about $1,833, so zinc supply is the main limit on earnings.

Prepare **80 containers of diced onions** and **60 containers of diced carrots**. This yields the maximum profit of **$1000**. Both peeling time (2000 minutes) and cutting time (2500 minutes) are fully used. Cutting time is the constraint that limits the result: removing it would let the solver find a better plan, even though adding more cutting minutes would not improve profit. Peeling time does not limit the result, since removing it would not improve the plan.

The company should make 7 foldable phones and 43 regular phones each week, which brings in a profit of $16,400. This uses all 150 software hours, and 1 of the 200 hardware hours is left over. Software hours are the bottleneck, but both limits affect the result: removing either constraint would let the model find a better plan. Still, giving the factory one more hour in either section would not raise the profit, because the whole-number requirement on phone counts means extra time can't be used to build another phone.

Make 2,000 Gilgamesh Supreme monitors and no Aleph 3 monitors. This plan yields the highest profit, $5,000,000. Assembly hours are fully used, and 1,500 packaging hours are left over. Assembly time is the constraint that limits the result: removing it would improve the profit, even though one more assembly hour would not improve it under the whole-number requirement. Packaging time does not limit the result, so the spare packaging hours have no effect on profit.

The factory should make about 10.29 kg of rice and 33.82 kg of corn, which yields a maximum profit of about $1,051.47. Machine work and sun-resting time are both used up completely, so they are the bottlenecks. Each extra machine hour would add about $4.71 to profit, and each extra hour of sun-resting time about $1.47. Human labor is not a constraint, with about 45.59 hours left unused, so adding more of it would not help. These results assume the stated hourly requirements and profits are exact and that the factory can produce fractional kilograms.

David should buy 2 bottles of coconut water and 1 bottle of blue energade, for a minimum cost of $11. This mix meets his magnesium and calcium needs exactly and leaves 5 units of potassium above his minimum. Magnesium is the constraint that limits the result: the cost would be lower without that requirement, and it would also drop if the requirement were relaxed by one unit. Potassium and calcium do not limit the result, since removing either requirement would not lower the cost.

Plant no strawberries and devote all 120 acres... no, plant 50 acres of watermelons and leave the rest of the farmland unplanted. This earns the maximum profit of $25,000. The spraying days are the bottleneck: every watermelon acre needs 2 spraying days, so the 100 days available are fully used. Each extra spraying day would add about $250 in profit, but George's land (70 acres unused) and watering days (140 unused) are not limiting anything.

Make 96 acrylic nail paints and no gel paints, for a monthly profit of $19,200. The mixing hours are fully used, and that is the constraint that caps production. Raw material hours (98 left over) and packing hours (289.2 left over) don't limit the result, since removing either one wouldn't improve the outcome. Mixing hours do limit it: removing that limit would let the solver find a better plan, and adding one more mixing hour wouldn't improve the whole-unit answer.

Put **$3,000 in GICs** and **$7,000 in the index ETF**. This mix earns the maximum expected return of **$585** for the year and meets both the $4,000 minimum ETF requirement and the 30% safe-GIC requirement. The plan is limited by two constraints: the full $10,000 is already used, and the GIC floor is exactly met, so the $3,000 in low-yield GICs is what holds the return down. Each extra dollar of budget would add about $0.075 in return, but each extra dollar required in GICs would cost about $0.055. The ETF minimum has $3,000 of room, so it does not limit the plan.

The lowest-cost plan is to hire no UI designers and 50 software engineers, for a weekly wage bill of $100000. This is the cheapest way to reach the 50-worker minimum, since engineers cost less per week than designers. The 50-worker minimum is the only constraint that limits the result: relaxing it would lower the bill, so the team size requirement drives the cost. The other rules (at least 10 engineers, engineers at least a third of designers, and the $200000 wage cap) are not limiting here, even though they have room to spare.

**What to do:** Make no bike tires and 100 car tires. **What it achieves:** This gives the highest profit the factory can reach, $2000. **What limits it:** The manufacturing machine time is fully used, and dropping that limit would allow a better result, so it is the constraint holding profit down. Adding one more unit of machine time would not raise profit, because whole tires can't be made from a fraction of a unit. The air-filling time has 50 units left over and doesn't limit the result, since neither loosening nor removing it would improve profit.

The best plan is to make 1,200 raincoats and no umbrellas, which gives the lowest total production cost of $8,400. This meets the weekly requirement of at least 1,200 items exactly, and raincoats are the cheaper item at $7 each versus $12 for umbrellas. The machine-hours requirement of at least 70 hours has 290 hours of slack, and the model says it does not limit the result, so the plan comfortably keeps the machine running. The 1,200-item minimum is what limits the result: the model says that lowering it would reduce cost, so the company's costs depend on that order requirement. Because the model uses whole-number quantities, these conclusions come from re-solving the model, not from the slack figures alone.

Make **38 regular packages and 39 premium packages**. This plan can treat **193 people**, the most the model finds under its rules. The rule that regular packages must be fewer than premium packages is the one that sets the mix, and the drying machine's time also limits the result: even with 20 seconds left over, removing that limit would let the model treat more people. Raising the drying limit by one unit would not help, but removing it entirely would. The herb supply does not limit the result, since 130 units go unused, and the minimum of 15 regular packages does not either, since 23 more than that are already made.

Use no drones and 32 couriers, which gives the minimum of 32 deliveries (the objective value). This exactly meets the 800-package requirement, and the cost is well within the budget, with $660 of the $1300 left unused. The package requirement is the constraint that limits the result: dropping it would reduce the count, so it is what forces the number up to 32. The budget and the drone limit do not limit the result, since removing either would not improve the answer, even though the drone limit leaves 32 units of slack.

Make 50 anti-inflammatory cream containers and 62 pain-killing cream containers. This uses 324 units of water, the lowest amount that meets the requirements. The minimum of 50 anti-inflammatory containers and the 55% pain-killing share both limit the result, and easing either one would reduce the water needed. The antibiotic supply does not limit it, since 914 units are left over.

Send 10 cars and 8 trucks, which uses the minimum of 212 units of gas that the model finds while meeting the flower requirement. This plan delivers at least 130 units with 2 units to spare, and it keeps cars above trucks by the required margin. Both rules limit the result: the objective would improve if the flower requirement were dropped or raised by one unit, and it would also improve if the cars-exceed-trucks rule were dropped. That rule has 1 unit of slack, but raising its limit wouldn't help, so the slack alone doesn't show that it's limiting the answer. Because the vehicles come in whole units, these re-solves are a more reliable guide than the slack amounts.

The child should eat 1 serving of fruit and 8 servings of juice each week. This gives the lowest total sugar, 121 units, while meeting the mineral and hydration targets and the rule of at least twice as much juice as fruit. The mineral requirement is what limits the result: dropping it would lower the sugar total, and allowing one more unit of mineral would also help. The "twice as much juice" rule also limits the result even though 6 units of slack remain, since dropping it would lower the sugar, but loosening it would not help. The hydration target does not limit the result, because neither dropping it nor loosening it changes the best plan, even though 11 units of hydration are left over.

Take 2 servings of the sleeping pills and 2 servings of the sleep supplement. This gives a sugar intake of 7.0 units, the lowest total that meets the sleepiness and discomfort limits with whole servings. Both limits still restrict the result, even though each has some room left: sleepiness is 1.0 unit above its minimum and discomfort is 0.7 unit below its maximum. Removing either limit would let the sugar total drop, and easing either one by a unit would also lower it, so the patient should treat both as real constraints.

Eat 2 salmon lunches and 7 bison burgers, which gives the lowest fat intake the model allows: 107 grams. The protein requirement doesn't restrict this choice, since the plan provides 80 grams more protein than needed. The carb requirement does restrict it: the plan meets it exactly, and dropping it would lower the fat total, though raising the carb target by one unit wouldn't help because meals come in whole units. The 25% salmon cap also limits the result, even though the plan leaves some room under it, because relaxing it by one unit would lower fat.

Make no batches of mixture A and about 42.86 batches of mixture B. This gives the largest total eruption, about 171.43 units. Vinegar is the limiting ingredient: all 300 units are used, so it caps the result. Each extra unit of vinegar would add about 0.57 units of eruption, while the leftover baking soda (about 28.57 units) and garbage allowance (about 17.14 units) would not help on their own.

Buy 10 ABC refrigerators and 5 XYZ refrigerators, for 15 units in total, the fewest that meets the store's rules. Schedule 115 tonometer tests and 112 "puff of air" tests, for a total of 227 patients. The office-hours limit is a real constraint: the 8-hour day is almost fully used (0.01 hours left), and adding more time would allow more patients. The rule that tonometer tests must exceed puff tests also limits the result, and relaxing it would help even though 2 tests of room remain. The minimum of 30 puff tests does not limit the result, since the plan uses 112, and removing that requirement would not improve the total. Note that the model counts eye-pressure checks, while the question asks about temperature checks, so the 227 applies to eye-pressure patients.

Schedule 50 dentist shifts and 80 oral hygienist shifts, for 130 shifts in total, which is the fewest that meets the requirements. This plan covers the 1000 labour hours exactly and uses the full $65,000 budget. The minimum of 20 dentist shifts is not what limits the plan, since 30 dentist shifts of slack remain above it. The labour-hours requirement and the budget are the real limits: loosening either by one unit would not improve the result because of whole-number shifts, but dropping either one would allow a better schedule.

Schedule **26 bike trips** and **11 car trips**, for a total of **1370 minutes**, the lowest possible under these rules. The plan meets the requirement of at least 850 orders and keeps bike trips at or above 70% of all trips, leaving 12 orders and 0.1 of bike-share margin unused. Both rules still limit the result, even with that margin: dropping either one would lower the total minutes, and loosening the bike-share rule would also improve it. Loosening the orders rule would not help by itself, so the bike-share rule is the tighter restriction.

The company should schedule **44 logging truck trips** and **43 lumber carrier vessel trips**, for a minimum total cost of **$54,000**. The trucks-exceed-vessels rule is fully used (trucks lead vessels by exactly 1), and it limits the result: easing that rule by one unit would lower the cost. The 300,000 lb lumber requirement has 2,000 lbs to spare, but it still limits the result because dropping it would lower the cost, and making it one unit easier would not help, since whole trips can't cover a smaller gap. So this plan is the cheapest option that keeps both the management rule and the lumber target.

Hire 46 full-time tutors and 208 assistant tutors, for 254 staff in total, which is the smallest headcount that still meets the Christmas-break need. This covers the required 1200 teaching hours exactly and stays within the $55,000 budget, with $140 to spare. The teaching-hours requirement is the main limit: it is fully used, and dropping it would change the result, so the hours target is what sets the headcount. The budget also limits the result even though $140 is left unused: removing the budget limit would improve the outcome, while raising the budget by one unit would not help, because whole-number hiring makes the leftover money too small to matter. Since the model requires whole numbers of people, the budget and hours limits interact, so the plan should be treated as the best whole-number mix, not an exact fractional one.

The patient should drink 17 glasses of protein shake and 51 glasses of milk, which gives the lowest sugar intake possible: 306 grams. The calcium requirement has 216 units to spare and doesn't restrict the result, since dropping it would not lower the sugar. The protein requirement and the rule that milk must be at least 3 times the shakes are both fully used, and removing either would allow less sugar, so both limit the plan. Loosening either limit by one unit would not lower the sugar further, because whole glasses only allow these exact amounts to work well.

Use **17 truck trips and 10 boat trips**, which gives the lowest pollution total of **1960**. This plan moves at least the required 1000 units, with 10 units to spare. The requirement to move the product and the 40% cap on boat trips both restrict the result: dropping either one would improve the pollution figure, even though the boat-share rule still has 0.8 of slack. Loosening the boat-share limit by one unit would also help, but loosening the product requirement by one unit would not, because the whole-number trips make a small change unhelpful. The minimum of 10 truck trips does not limit the result, since dropping it would not improve the pollution figure and the plan already uses 7 more truck trips than that minimum.

Do 7 hydraulics experiments and no force experiments. This gives a total excitement of 35. Solid and gas are not limiting, since the result would not improve with either dropped or loosened, so the lab has plenty of them to spare.

The sugar limit is the main constraint: raising the cap by one gram would not help because scoops come in whole units, but removing the limit would raise the protein total, so it is what holds the result back. The rule that vanilla must be at least twice the chocolate also limits the result, even though 2 scoops of slack remain, since dropping it would improve the total. The minimum of 2 chocolate scoops does not limit the result.

Both requirements are met exactly, with no extra capacity left over. Each additional water sample required would add about 0.1 units of heat, and each additional dirt sample about 0.05 units, so these two sample requirements are what limit how low the heat can go.

The wood supply, the limit of 3 cars, and the rule requiring more trucks than cars are not limiting the result, since none of them would improve the outcome if removed.

Hire 24 architects and 23 drafters each week to complete 71 projects, the most the budget and staffing rule allow. The one-more-architect-than-drafter rule is exactly met, so it sets the mix. The weekly budget leaves 400 dollars unspent, but it still limits the result: removing it entirely would allow a better plan, though adding one unit to its limit would not help because hires come in whole people. Likewise, the supervision rule limits the result, since dropping it would improve the outcome even though loosening it by one more unit would not.

Run 5 shuttle buses and 43 taxis, which covers all 250 workers (35 on buses plus 215 in taxis) for a total cost of $2250. Both the worker requirement and the 5-bus cap are fully used, and the cap is the limit that matters most: raising it would lower the cost. The worker requirement also limits the result. Adding one more worker to the requirement wouldn't reduce cost, but dropping the requirement entirely would, so it is what keeps the cost from being lower. Because the model requires whole vehicles, the plan is only as good as these two limits allow.

The plant should process 20 liquid waste batches and 10 solid waste batches, which serves 230 people, the most possible under these rules. The disinfectant and bacteria supplies do not limit the result, since 650 units of disinfectant and 450 units of bacteria go unused and extra supply of either would not help.

The budget and the rule that trucks must be fewer than vans do not limit the result, since removing either would not improve it, even though $1500 of the budget and a gap of 19 transports go unused.

Making one more unit of either limit wouldn't raise revenue, but removing either limit would, so both are real constraints on the result. Schedule 7 expert shifts and 54 apprentice shifts. This covers the required 5,000 square meters at the lowest total cost, 19,700 dollars. The glucose requirement does not limit the result, since removing it would not help and neither would loosening it, and the plan already delivers 20 units more glucose medicine than required.

Run Method Y 108.3 times and don't run Method X at all. This yields about 75.83 units of the desired element, the most possible with the available materials. The plan is only as good as the 6 manual and 15 electric jacks the company actually has access to.

Use 4 medium containers and 12 large containers, which keeps the number of large containers at three times the number of medium ones. This gives the lowest weekly checking workload of 44 checks.
